Refractive index is the ratio of the speed in vacuum to the speed in the medium, and
both speeds come from the same formula.
**Step 1 — write the two speeds.**
in vacuum: c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀)
in the medium: v = 1/√(µε) ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio.**
n = c/v
= √(µε)/√(µ₀ε₀)
= **√[µε/(µ₀ε₀)]** ✓
**Step 3 — recognise the familiar form.** Writing µ_r = µ/µ₀ and ε_r = ε/ε₀,
**n = √(µ_r ε_r)** ✓ - Maxwell's relation.
**Why the index is a square root.** Wave speed always depends on the **square root** of
the medium's constants, just as v = √(T/µ) for a string ✓ The index inherits that root.
**A worked instance.** For water at optical frequencies, µ_r ≈ 1 and ε_r ≈ 1·77:
n = √1·77 = **1·33** ✓ the familiar value.
**Why µ_r is usually dropped.** For almost all transparent materials µ_r differs from 1
by less than a part in a thousand ✓ so n ≈ √ε_r - which is Maxwell's relation in its
usual form, and one of the first great confirmations that light is an electromagnetic
wave.
**The caution about frequency.** The ε_r measured at low frequency does not give the
optical index ✓ Water has ε_r = 80 statically, which would predict n = 8·9; but the
molecules cannot rotate fast enough to follow an optical field, so the effective ε_r
falls to 1·77.
**What the formula tells us about speed.** A larger n means a **smaller** v ✓ Light
slows in a medium because the oscillating field polarises the atoms, and their
re-radiation interferes with the original wave to retard it.
**Checking the dimensions.** µ_r and ε_r are both dimensionless, so n is dimensionless ✓
as a refractive index must be.
**A special case worth knowing.** For a **metamaterial** with both µ and ε negative,
the square root must be taken with a **negative** sign, giving a negative refractive
index ✓ Light then bends the "wrong" way at the interface.
**Reading the distractors.** **√(µ₀ε₀/µε)** ✗ is 1/n, which would be less than 1 for a
dense medium - impossible for a refractive index. The remaining options mix µ and ε₀,
which is dimensionally inconsistent ✓
∴ √[µε/(µ₀ε₀)].

The object lies **between f and 2f**, which gives a real, inverted, magnified image.
**Step 1 — find the focal length.**
f = R/2 = 15/2 = **7·5 cm** ✓ and for a concave mirror it is taken as negative in the
Cartesian convention: f = −7·5 cm.
**Step 2 — locate the object.** It is at **10 cm**, which lies **between** f = 7·5 cm
and 2f = 15 cm ✓ - the region that produces a magnified real image.
**Step 3 — apply the mirror formula.** With u = −10 cm and f = −7·5 cm:
1/v + 1/u = 1/f
1/v = −1/7·5 + 1/10
= (−4 + 3)/30
= **−1/30**
**v = −30 cm** ✓ negative, so the image is **real** and on the same side as the object.
**Step 4 — find the magnification.**
m = −v/u
= −(−30)/(−10)
= **−3** ✓
The magnitude 3 means **magnified** three times; the minus sign means **inverted**.
**Step 5 — state the image.** **Magnified and inverted**, 30 cm high ✓
**The six standard cases for a concave mirror.**
object beyond C: image between F and C, **real, inverted, diminished**
object at C (2f): image at C, **real, inverted, same size**
object between F and C: image beyond C, **real, inverted, magnified** ✓ our case
object at F: image at **infinity**
object inside F: image behind the mirror, **virtual, erect, magnified** ✓
**Why a real image must be inverted.** Rays actually cross in front of the mirror ✓ An
**erect** image from a concave mirror is always **virtual**, formed when the object is
inside the focus - which is how a shaving or make-up mirror works.
**The image size.** 3 x 10 cm = **30 cm** tall, inverted ✓
**A quick way to classify.** Compare the object distance with f and 2f ✓ Between them
means magnified and real; beyond 2f means diminished and real; inside f means virtual
and erect. No arithmetic is needed to choose among the options.
**Reading the distractors.** **Magnified and erect** ✗ would need the object inside the
focus, at under 7·5 cm. **Diminished and inverted** ✗ needs it beyond 15 cm.
**Diminished and erect** ✗ describes a **convex** mirror ✓
∴ magnified and inverted.

A paraxial ray **parallel to the principal axis** reflects **through the focus**.
**Step 1 — identify the incident ray.** PQ runs **horizontally**, parallel to the
principal axis, and strikes the mirror at Q ✓ The question states it is **paraxial** -
close enough to the axis for the standard rules to apply.
**Step 2 — apply the rule for a concave mirror.** Of the standard construction rays,
the one parallel to the axis is reflected so that it **passes through the principal
focus F** ✓
**Step 3 — pick the ray.** Of the four reflected rays drawn, the one heading from Q
**through F** is ray **C** ✓
**Why this rule holds.** A concave mirror is designed - ideally as a paraboloid - to
bring all rays parallel to its axis to a single point, the focus ✓ For a spherical
mirror it holds only for **paraxial** rays, which is exactly why the question
specifies that PQ is one.
**The four standard construction rays.**
parallel to the axis → reflects **through F** ✓
through **F** → reflects **parallel** to the axis ✓
through the **centre of curvature C** → reflects **back along itself**, since it meets
the mirror normally ✓
striking the **pole** → reflects symmetrically about the axis ✓
Any two of these locate an image.
**Checking the other rays against the laws of reflection.**
ray **A**, heading up and away ✗ - it diverges from the axis, which a concave mirror
cannot do to an incoming parallel ray
ray **B**, back towards the left above the axis ✗ - it misses the focus entirely
ray **D**, straight down ✗ - that would need the mirror surface at Q to be at 45°,
which it is not ✓
**What happens to non-paraxial rays.** They cross the axis **nearer** the mirror than F,
producing **spherical aberration** ✓ which is why large telescopes use **parabolic**
mirrors, for which the focusing is exact at all heights.
**Why the focus is at R/2.** For a paraxial ray at height h, the geometry of the
reflection gives the crossing point at **R/2** from the pole, independent of h ✓
∴ C.

At the critical angle, sin θ is the **ratio of the speeds**, so the speed in B follows
at once.
**Step 1 — write the critical-angle condition.**
sin θ = n_B/n_A ✓
with A the denser medium.
**Step 2 — convert the indices to speeds.** Since n = c/v,
n_B/n_A = (c/v_B)/(c/v_A)
= **v_A/v_B** ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
sin θ = v_A/v_B
so
**v_B = v_A/sin θ = V/sin θ** ✓
**Why v_B must be the larger.** Total internal reflection happens only going from
**denser to rarer**, and the rarer medium is where light travels **faster** ✓ Since
sin θ < 1, dividing by it **increases** V - as it must.
**A worked instance.** With θ = 30°:
v_B = V/0·5 = **2V** ✓
and the indices are in the ratio n_A/n_B = 2, so A is twice as optically dense as B.
**The formula in all its forms.**
sin θ = n_B/n_A = v_A/v_B = λ_A/λ_B ✓
all three ratios being equal - a useful set to have at hand.
**A check on the limits.**
θ → 90°: sin θ → 1 and v_B → **V**, so the two media are identical and there is no
refraction at all ✓
θ small: v_B is **much** larger than V, meaning a very large index contrast - which is
why diamond, with its 24° critical angle, traps light so effectively ✓
**Why this is the basis of optical fibres.** Light launched into the core at a shallow
enough angle strikes the cladding beyond the critical angle and is reflected with
**100%** efficiency ✓ Repeated thousands of times, it carries the signal for
kilometres.
**How to measure a refractive index with it.** Observe the angle at which the refracted
beam just disappears ✓ Then n = 1/sin C for a medium in air - the principle of the
Abbe refractometer.
**Reading the distractors.** **V/cos θ** ✗ uses the wrong trigonometric function.
**V(1 − sin θ)** ✗ and **V(1 − cos θ)** ✗ would make v_B **smaller** than V, so light
would travel more slowly in the rarer medium - impossible ✓
∴ V/sin θ.

For a transistor to work as an amplifier, the emitter-base junction is **forward**
biased and the collector-base junction **reverse** biased.
**Step 1 — see why the emitter junction is forward biased.** Its job is to **inject**
carriers into the base ✓ A forward bias lowers that junction's barrier so that a large
current of majority carriers - electrons in an n-p-n - flows from emitter into base.
**Step 2 — see why the collector junction is reverse biased.** Its job is to **collect**
those carriers ✓ The reverse bias creates a strong field across the junction that
sweeps any carrier reaching it straight into the collector, and keeps the collector
current almost independent of the collector voltage.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Forward, reverse** ✓ - the **active** region, where a
transistor amplifies.
**Why the base must be thin and lightly doped.** So that almost all the injected
carriers cross it without recombining ✓ Typically **95 to 99%** reach the collector,
and only the small remainder leaves as base current. That ratio is what gives current
gain:
β = I_C/I_B, often **100** or more ✓
**Where the amplification comes from.** The same current passes from a **low-resistance**
forward-biased input to a **high-resistance** reverse-biased output ✓ Since
P = I²R, the power is greatly increased - and that is the whole principle. The name
**trans**fer-re**sistor** records it.
**The four possible biasing combinations.**
forward, reverse: **active** - amplification ✓
forward, forward: **saturation** - the transistor is fully on, a closed switch ✓
reverse, reverse: **cut-off** - fully off, an open switch ✓
reverse, forward: **reverse active** - a poor amplifier, rarely used
Digital circuits swing between saturation and cut-off; analogue ones stay in the active
region.
**Why the collector is made larger than the emitter.** It must dissipate the heat
generated as carriers are swept across the reverse-biased junction ✓ which is why
transistors are not symmetric despite looking so in the circuit symbol.
**Reading the distractors.** **Reverse, forward** ✗ is the inverted mode. **Forward,
forward** ✗ is saturation, and **reverse, reverse** ✗ is cut-off ✓ None of the three
amplifies.
∴ forward, reverse.

Forward bias **opposes** the built-in field, so the potential barrier is **reduced** but
still rises from p to n.
**Step 1 — recall the unbiased junction.** Diffusion of carriers leaves a depletion
region with fixed charges, creating a built-in potential ✓ The n side sits at a
**higher** potential than the p side - a step of about **0·7 V** for silicon.
**Step 2 — apply forward bias.** The external supply makes the p side **positive** and
the n side **negative** ✓ This opposes the built-in field, so the barrier height
**falls**.
**Step 3 — see what the graph must show.** Still a step **upward** from p to n, since
the barrier is reduced rather than reversed, but a **smaller** one than before ✓ That
is the second graph.
**Why the barrier cannot reverse.** The applied voltage is less than the built-in
potential in normal operation ✓ If it exceeded it, the junction would conduct
enormously and the diode would be destroyed; in practice the current rises so steeply
near 0·7 V that the barrier never quite vanishes.
**What the reduced barrier does.** Many more carriers now have enough thermal energy to
surmount it, so the diffusion current rises **exponentially** ✓
I = I₀[e^(eV/kT) − 1] ✓
the diode equation - which is why the forward characteristic turns on so sharply.
**What reverse bias does instead.** It **adds** to the built-in field, raising the
barrier and **widening** the depletion region ✓ The graph would then show a **taller**
step, and only a tiny leakage current flows.
**The depletion width.** It **narrows** under forward bias and **widens** under
reverse ✓ That voltage-dependent width is what gives a reverse-biased junction its
capacitance - exploited in the **varactor** diode used to tune radios.
**A caution about the graph's axes.** The vertical axis is **potential**, not current ✓
The step's **height** is the barrier, and the step's **width** the depletion region. A
graph sloping downward from p to n would describe a quite different device.
**Reading the distractors.** A **larger** step ✗ is reverse bias. A step the **same**
size ✗ is the unbiased junction. A **downward** step ✗ would mean the p side at higher
potential, which no ordinary bias produces ✓
∴ the second graph - a reduced step rising from p to n.

Aluminium and indium are **both trivalent**, so both act as acceptors and the crystal
becomes **p-type**.
**Step 1 — place the dopants in the periodic table.** Both aluminium and indium are in
**group 13** ✓ Each has **three** valence electrons, one fewer than germanium's four.
**Step 2 — see what a trivalent atom does in the lattice.** It forms three covalent
bonds and leaves the fourth **incomplete** ✓ That vacancy is a **hole**, able to accept
an electron from a neighbouring bond and so move through the crystal.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Both dopants supply holes, so the crystal becomes **p-type**,
with holes as the **majority** carriers ✓
**Why "equal numbers" is a red herring.** Equal numbers of **two acceptors** simply
means twice as many acceptors ✓ Their effects **add** rather than cancel. Had one been
trivalent and the other **pentavalent** - say aluminium and antimony - they would
compensate, and equal numbers would leave the crystal intrinsic.
**What compensation would look like.** N_D = N_A gives a **compensated** semiconductor,
behaving almost like the pure material ✓ That is the trap this question sets, and the
first option states it.
**The energy-level picture.** Each acceptor creates a level just **above** the valence
band - about **0·01 eV** in germanium ✓ Electrons from the valence band are easily
promoted into it even at room temperature, leaving mobile holes behind.
**Why doping transforms conductivity.** Pure germanium has about 10¹⁹ carriers per cubic
metre; doping at one part in a million adds some 10²² ✓ a thousandfold increase in
conductivity, and complete control over it.
**Why the crystal stays electrically neutral.** Each acceptor atom is itself neutral
when added ✓ Once it accepts an electron it becomes a fixed **negative ion**, balanced
exactly by the mobile positive hole. The material has mobile positive carriers but no
net charge.
**The minority carriers.** Electrons, present in small numbers from thermal generation ✓
Their concentration satisfies np = n_i², so adding holes **reduces** the electron
population.
**Reading the distractors.** "**n-type**" ✗ would need **pentavalent** dopants such as
phosphorus or arsenic. "**Remains intrinsic**" ✗ would need compensation by opposite
dopants. "**Insulator**" ✗ is the reverse of what doping does ✓
∴ it becomes a p-type semiconductor.
